newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Germany seen reasserting commitment to EMU.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany seen reasserting commitment to EMU.

text.p: Top French and German finance officials are expected to reassert on Wednesday their commitment to launching a single European currency in 1999, amid resurgent speculation about a delay to the birth of the euro.

A French finance ministry official said that Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, and central bank heads Jean-Claude Trichet and Hans Tietmeyer would discuss the economic outlook and progress towards monetary union when they met in the central French city of Lyon.

He played down speculation that Germany's difficulties in cutting its budget deficit to meet Maastricht treaty criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) might make it hard to launch the euro in 1999.
"France and Germany will be in. There has been no declaration from the German government to suggest that it has changed its position," he said.

Despite a string of comments from senior German officials -- most recently from three Bundesbank council members on Monday -- that EMU could and should start on time, Bonn's problems in cutting its deficit have encouraged disquiet about the process.
German economist Herbert Hax, an adviser to the German government, fanned that unease over the weekend by calling for a delay to EMU, arguing that Germany would miss the entry rules.
Germany needs a way of achieving EMU entry for itself while insisting on a strict enough interpretation of the Maastricht treaty to keep out Italy and other southern European Union countries.
Bonn is believed to be reluctant to allow in Italy, Spain and Portugal at the start of monetary union, fearing this might undermine the euro's credibility at its launch.

Wednesday's talks, due to last just over two hours, will see France in the unusual position of being on stronger ground than Germany. Paris is likely to cut its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year.
"All of a sudden we are a lot less worried about France meeting the criteria and more worried about Germany," said Marie Owens-Thomsen, economist at BIP-Dresdner in Paris.

But economists say France has little reason to gloat over Germany's troubles, as any threat to the single currency would undermine a project on which the French government has staked its entire policy and reputation.

French officials say there can be no question of delaying monetary union as this would mean amending the Maastricht treaty -- implying reopening negotiations, new parliamentary debates and new referenda, all of which could put off EMU for years.
"Everyone has something to lose. Whatever the economics of it, the most workable compromise is for it to go ahead with a small group of countries," said UBS economist Darren Williams.
A launch by a small group in 1999 would be accompanied by a face-saving declaration pledging to bring Italy and others into EMU before notes and coins go into circulation in 2002.
The French official said Wednesday's talks would also touch on France's proposal for a stability council to co-ordinate economic policies inside the euro zone.
Germany agrees in principle with the idea, although details need to be ironed out, amid concern about the division of power between it and the European Central Bank.
The two sides would also discuss tax harmonisation before a ministerial meeting in May of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the official said.
